title: Interview Prep, Comparisons and Best Practices

topics.title: Express Interview Questions: Rapid-Fire Round
topics.summary: A compact set of the most common Express and Node backend interview questions with crisp answers and a coding exercise.
topics.description:
Use this page as a last-minute revision sheet. Say the short answer first, then add one detail or example.

| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| What is middleware? | A function `(req, res, next)` in the request pipeline; it can change req/res, end the request or call `next()`. |
| Order of middleware? | Registration order; parsers and security first, routes, 404, error handler last. |
| `app.use` vs `app.get`? | `use` matches every method and any path prefix; `get` matches only GET on the exact route. |
| `req.params` vs `req.query` vs `req.body`? | Path segments, the part after `?`, and the parsed payload. |
| How do you handle errors? | Throw or `next(err)`; one 4-argument error handler at the end; Express 5 forwards rejected promises. |
| 401 vs 403? | Not authenticated vs authenticated but not allowed. |
| What is CORS? | A browser rule; the server sends `Access-Control-*` headers to allow other origins. |
| JWT vs sessions? | JWT is stateless and hard to revoke; sessions are server-side and easy to revoke. |
| How to store passwords? | Hash with bcrypt/argon2 (salted, slow); never encrypt or use SHA-256 alone. |
| How to prevent NoSQL injection? | Validate types (strings only), whitelist fields, `sanitizeFilter`, never pass raw `req.body` to queries. |
| Why is Node fast for I/O? | Non-blocking event loop; but CPU-heavy work blocks all requests. |
| How do you scale Express? | Stateless app, multiple processes (PM2/containers), load balancer, Redis for shared state, caching. |
| What is `next('route')`? | Skip the remaining handlers of the current route. |
| How do you structure a project? | Routes -> controllers -> services -> models, config module, central errors. |

### How to answer scenario questions
State the **problem**, the **approach**, the **trade-off** and how you would **test** it. For example: "To protect login from brute force I add a strict rate limit per IP and account, return a generic error, hash with bcrypt, and log failures."

### Coding exercise
Interviewers love asking for a hand-written middleware such as a rate limiter, a logger, or `asyncHandler`. Practise the one in the example: it keeps per-key counters in a Map and answers 429 after the limit.
keyPoints: Explain middleware, order, error handling and the req/res cycle fluently
Security basics: bcrypt, JWT/sessions, CORS, helmet, validation, rate limiting
Be ready to write a small middleware (logger, auth, rate limiter) live
Discuss scaling: stateless design, PM2/containers, Redis, caching
pitfalls: Memorising definitions without being able to show code
Saying "JWT is encrypted" or "CORS protects the server"
Ignoring error paths when writing live code

interview.q: Explain the Express request lifecycle in an interview-ready way.
interview.a: A request enters Express, passes through global middleware in order (security, logging, parsers), reaches the first matching route and its handlers, and ends with a res method; if nothing matches the 404 handler responds, and any thrown or next(err) error is sent to the error-handling middleware.

interview.q: How would you design login security for an Express API?
interview.a: Validate input, hash passwords with bcrypt, return generic errors, rate-limit by IP and account, issue short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies, use HTTPS, and log failed attempts.

interview.q: Why is blocking the event loop dangerous?
interview.a: Node runs JavaScript on one thread, so a long synchronous task (huge loops, sync crypto, large JSON parsing) delays every other request; move CPU-heavy work to workers or queues.

interview.q: What is the difference between process.nextTick, setImmediate and a promise callback?
interview.a: nextTick runs before the event loop continues (highest priority), promise callbacks run in the microtask queue right after, and setImmediate runs in the check phase after I/O callbacks.

topics.title: Express vs Fastify vs Koa vs NestJS
topics.summary: Compare the main Node web frameworks by philosophy, speed, features and when each is the right choice.
topics.description:
All four run on Node's `http` module, but they make different trade-offs.

| | Express | Fastify | Koa | NestJS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Style | minimal, callbacks/async | plugin-based, schema-first | minimal, async/await "onion" | opinionated, TypeScript, DI |
| Built-ins | routing, static, few helpers | validation + serialization via JSON Schema, logging (pino) | almost nothing (needs router/body modules) | modules, controllers, guards, pipes, ORM integrations |
| Performance | good | very high (often 2-3x Express in benchmarks) | good | depends on adapter (Express or Fastify) |
| Ecosystem | largest, most tutorials | large and growing | smaller | large, enterprise |
| Learning curve | easiest | easy-moderate | easy | steepest |

### Express
Most popular, huge middleware ecosystem, perfect for learning, MERN and small to mid-size APIs. You design the architecture yourself. Express 5 modernised async handling.

### Fastify
Choose it when throughput and low overhead matter, or when you want built-in validation and fast JSON serialisation from schemas. Plugins are encapsulated, which keeps large codebases tidy. Many Express ideas map directly (routes, hooks instead of middleware).

### Koa
By the Express authors: tiny core, `ctx` object, middleware that can `await next()` and run code before **and** after downstream handlers. Great for those who want a bare toolkit.

### NestJS
Angular-style architecture (modules, decorators, dependency injection) on top of Express or Fastify. Best for large teams and long-lived enterprise apps that need strong conventions and testability. More boilerplate.

### Rule of thumb
Learning, startups, quick APIs: **Express**. Performance-critical or schema-driven services: **Fastify**. Large TypeScript teams: **NestJS**. Minimal custom stacks: **Koa**.
keyPoints: Express: biggest ecosystem and easiest to learn; you choose the architecture
Fastify: fastest, schema validation/serialization built in, plugin encapsulation
Koa: tiny async/await core with an onion middleware model
NestJS: opinionated TypeScript framework with DI that can run on Express or Fastify
Pick by team size, performance needs and need for structure
pitfalls: Choosing a framework only from micro-benchmarks (database and network dominate real latency)
Expecting NestJS to replace Express knowledge (it sits on top of it)

examples.title: Same endpoint in Express, Fastify and Koa
NestJS controller

interview.q: When would you choose Fastify over Express?
interview.a: When performance and low overhead matter or you want schema-based validation and serialization out of the box; the trade-off is a smaller ecosystem of drop-in middleware.

interview.q: What is the main difference between Express and Koa middleware?
interview.a: Koa middleware are async functions using await next() so they can run code both before and after downstream handlers (an onion model) and share a ctx object, whereas Express uses (req, res, next) callbacks.

interview.q: Is NestJS a replacement for Express?
interview.a: No. NestJS is a higher-level framework that uses Express (or Fastify) underneath and adds structure such as modules, decorators and dependency injection.

topics.title: Migrating from Express 4 to 5
topics.summary: A checklist of the breaking changes in Express 5 with before/after code and the tools that help.
topics.description:
Express 5 is mostly compatible, but a few changes will break old code. Upgrade steps: use Node 18+, `npm install express@5`, run the codemod, then fix the items below and run your tests.

### Breaking changes checklist
| Area | Express 4 | Express 5 |
|---|---|---|
| Wildcards | `app.get('*', ...)` | `app.get('/*splat', ...)` or `/{*splat}` |
| Optional params | `/:id?` | braces: `/books{/:id}` |
| Inline param regex | `/:id(\d+)` | removed - validate in code |
| Async errors | need `try/catch` + `next(err)` | rejected promises are forwarded automatically |
| `req.query` | writable, parsed with `qs` | getter, parsed by the `simple` parser |
| `req.body` | `{}` when not parsed | `undefined` when not parsed |
| `express.urlencoded` | `extended: true` default | `extended: false` default |
| Removed methods | `app.del()`, `req.param()`, `res.sendfile()` | use `app.delete()`, `req.params/query/body`, `res.sendFile()` |
| `res.json(status, obj)` / `res.send(status)` | worked | **silently sends the number as the body** - use `res.status(n).json(obj)` |
| `res.redirect('back')` | back to referrer | no longer special - use `req.get('Referer') ?? '/'` |
| `res.status(x)` | any value | must be an integer 100-999 |
| `req.host` | hostname only | includes the port (`req.hostname` has none) |
| `app.listen(cb)` | cb ignored errors | cb receives the error (e.g. `EADDRINUSE`) |

### Tooling
`npx @expressjs/codemod upgrade` automates many mechanical edits (check the official migration guide for the current list). Also update middleware packages (`body-parser`, `cookie-parser`, `express-session`, `cors`, `multer`, `express-mongo-sanitize`/`hpp` compatibility) and check each package's changelog for Express 5 support.

### Strategy
Upgrade on a branch, search the code for the patterns above (`'*'`, `.del(`, `res.json(` with two arguments, `req.param(`), run your test suite, then deploy gradually.
keyPoints: Requires Node 18+; run `npx @expressjs/codemod upgrade`
Rename wildcards (`*splat`) and optional params (braces); drop inline regex
Remove v4-only helpers: `app.del`, `req.param`, `res.sendfile`, `res.json(status, body)`
Check body parsing (`req.body` undefined) and `req.query` assumptions
Async handlers no longer need wrappers
pitfalls: `res.send(404)` or `res.json(200, obj)` do NOT fail in v5: they respond 200 with the number as the body
Server crashes at startup with `PathError` because of an old route string

examples.title: Before and after
examples.code:
// ---------- Express 4 ----------
app.get('*', (req, res) => res.status(404).send('Not found'))
app.get('/users/:id?', handler)
app.get('/orders/:id(\\d+)', handler)
app.del('/posts/:id', removePost)
app.get('/old', (req, res) => res.json(200, { ok: true }))
app.get('/err', (req, res) => res.send(404))

// ---------- Express 5 ----------
app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).send('Not found'))        // or app.get('/{*splat}', ...)
app.get('/users{/:id}', handler)
app.get('/orders/:id', (req, res, next) => {
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(req.params.id)) return next('route')        // validate in code
  handler(req, res, next)
})
app.delete('/posts/:id', removePost)
app.get('/old', (req, res) => res.status(200).json({ ok: true }))
app.get('/err', (req, res) => res.sendStatus(404))

examples.title: What silently changes (verified behaviour)
examples.code:
# Express 5 server still running v4-style code:
curl -i localhost:3000/old
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# 200                      <-- the NUMBER 200 was sent as the body, your object vanished

curl -i localhost:3000/err
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK          <-- not 404!
# 404

# crash on startup for an old wildcard:
# PathError [TypeError]: Missing parameter name at index 5: /old*

interview.q: What is the biggest benefit of Express 5 for developers?
interview.a: Native promise support: rejected promises and thrown errors in async handlers reach the error middleware without wrappers, which removes a common source of hanging requests.

interview.q: How do you write a catch-all route in Express 5?
interview.a: Use a named wildcard like /{*splat} (or /*splat for non-root), or simply a final app.use middleware; the bare '*' pattern is invalid.

topics.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
topics.summary: The recurring bugs seen in Express code reviews and the habits that prevent them.
topics.description:
Most production incidents come from a short list of mistakes. Learn them once and review your code against them.

### Top mistakes
1. **Forgetting `next()` or a response** - request hangs.
2. **Sending two responses** - missing `return` after an early reply.
3. **Registering things in the wrong order** - routes before `express.json()`, 404 before routes, error handler not last.
4. **No central error handling** - try/catch repeated everywhere, leaking stack traces.
5. **Trusting input** - passing `req.body`/`req.query` directly into the database or `new Model(req.body)`.
6. **Weak auth** - plain or fast-hashed passwords, JWTs in `localStorage`, `alg` not pinned, secrets committed to git.
7. **Missing authorization** - checking only that the user is logged in, not that the resource is theirs (IDOR).
8. **Blocking the event loop** - sync file/crypto calls, huge loops in handlers.
9. **Connecting to the DB per request** instead of once at startup.
10. **CORS misuse** - `origin: '*'` with credentials, or enabling CORS "to fix" an error without understanding it.
11. **Unbounded responses** - lists without pagination; no body size limit.
12. **No `NODE_ENV=production`, no graceful shutdown, no health check.**

### Best-practice summary
- Layered structure; thin controllers; services for business rules.
- Validate everything with schemas; return consistent JSON errors with correct codes.
- Use helmet, rate limiting, HTTPS, httpOnly cookies, bcrypt, short-lived tokens.
- Keep secrets in env vars; validate config at startup.
- Log structured JSON with request ids; never log secrets.
- Write integration tests with supertest; run them in CI.
- Handle SIGTERM, close connections, and let a process manager restart crashes.
- Document the API (OpenAPI) and version it.
keyPoints: Always end the request exactly once; `return` after early responses
Middleware order: security, parsers, routes, 404, error handler
Validate input, authorize per resource, use a central error handler
Connect to the DB once; never block the event loop
Production: env vars, logging, health checks, tests, graceful shutdown
pitfalls: Fixing a failing request by disabling security (CORS `*`, removing auth) instead of finding the cause
Copy-pasting tutorial code that stores secrets or tokens insecurely

examples.title: Bad vs good handler
Pre-launch checklist
examples.code:
[ ] NODE_ENV=production, trust proxy set behind nginx/load balancer
[ ] helmet, CORS allow-list, rate limit on /auth/*, body size limits
[ ] All input validated; ownership checks on every resource route
[ ] Passwords hashed (bcrypt cost 12+), secrets in env, .env not in git
[ ] Central error handler: no stack traces in responses
[ ] Structured logs with request id; /health and /ready endpoints
[ ] DB indexes for filters/sorts; pagination on every list
[ ] Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM; process manager or container restart policy
[ ] npm audit clean; dependencies pinned with a lockfile
[ ] Tests (supertest) pass in CI; API docs published

interview.q: What are the three most common Express bugs you have seen?
interview.a: Requests that hang because next() or a response is missing, double responses from a missing return, and trusting req.body/req.params without validation or ownership checks.

interview.q: What goes wrong if you register express.json() after your routes?
interview.a: The routes run before the body is parsed, so req.body is undefined (in Express 5) and handlers fail or validate nothing.

interview.q: Why should every list endpoint be paginated?
interview.a: Without limits a single request can load an entire collection, exhausting memory and bandwidth and creating an easy denial-of-service vector.
